title: Old Sultan
paragraphs: A shepherd had a faithful dog named Sultan, who had grown very old and lost all his teeth. One day the shepherd and his wife were standing together in front of the house, and the shepherd said, “I’m going to shoot old Sultan tomorrow morning. He’s no use to anyone now.” But his wife said, “Please let the poor loyal creature live. He has served us well for many years, and we ought to keep him fed for the rest of his days.” “But what can we do with him?” said the shepherd. “He hasn’t a tooth in his head, and the thieves aren’t afraid of him at all. He has served us, it’s true, but he did it to earn his keep. Tomorrow is his last day, you can count on it.”

Poor Sultan was lying close by and heard everything the shepherd and his wife said to each other. He was terrified to think that tomorrow would be his last day, so that evening he went to his good friend the wolf, who lived in the wood, and told him all his troubles and how his master meant to kill him in the morning. “Don’t worry,” said the wolf. “I’ll give you some good advice. Every morning, very early, your master goes out to the field with his wife, and they take their little child along and lay it down in the shade behind the hedge while they work. Now, you lie down close beside the child and act as if you’re watching over it. I’ll come out of the wood and carry it off, and you must run after me as fast as you can. I’ll drop it, and then you can carry it back. They’ll think you saved their child, and they’ll be so grateful that they’ll look after you as long as you live.” The dog thought this was an excellent plan, and it was carried out just so. The wolf ran off a little way with the child, and the shepherd and his wife screamed, but Sultan soon caught up and carried the poor little thing back to his master and mistress. Then the shepherd patted him on the head and said, “Old Sultan has saved our child from the wolf, so he shall live and be well looked after and have plenty to eat. Wife, go home and give him a good dinner, and let him have my old cushion to sleep on for as long as he lives.” From then on Sultan had everything he could wish for.

Soon afterward the wolf came to congratulate him. “Now, my good fellow,” he said, “you must keep quiet and look the other way when I want a taste of one of the old shepherd’s fine fat sheep.” “No,” said Sultan. “I will be true to my master.” The wolf thought he was joking, though, and came one night looking for a tasty bite. But Sultan had told his master what the wolf intended, so the shepherd lay in wait for him behind the barn door. While the wolf was busy picking out a fat sheep, the shepherd laid a heavy stick across his back and gave his coat a thorough combing.

The wolf was furious. He called Sultan “an old rogue” and swore he would get his revenge. Next morning he sent the boar to challenge Sultan to meet in the wood and settle the matter. Sultan had no one to ask to be his second except the shepherd’s old three-legged cat. So he took her along, and as the poor thing hobbled painfully on, she held her tail straight up in the air.

The wolf and the wild boar reached the spot first. When they saw their enemies approaching, with the cat’s long tail sticking straight up, they thought she was carrying a sword for Sultan to fight with. Every time she limped, they thought she was bending down to pick up a stone to throw at them. They decided they didn’t care for this kind of fighting, so the boar lay down behind a bush and the wolf jumped up into a tree. Sultan and the cat arrived, looked around, and wondered why nobody was there. The boar, however, had not hidden himself completely, because his ears were sticking out of the bush. When he twitched one of them a little, the cat saw something move and, thinking it was a mouse, pounced on it, biting and scratching, so that the boar leaped up, grunting, and ran off, bellowing, “Look up in the tree. The one to blame is sitting there!” So they looked up and spotted the wolf sitting among the branches. They called him a cowardly rascal and would not let him come down until he was thoroughly ashamed of himself and had promised to be good friends with old Sultan again.
